Comfortable
cum'fort-a-bl
a. (giving comfort; strengthening; in the Authorized Version, of words that put heart into a man)
From comfort, Old French conforter, from Latin confortare, to strengthen greatly, from con- and fortis, strong. The root is strength, not ease — a fact the modern English has entirely lost.

Biblical Definition

Modern English hears comfortable and thinks of a chair. The Authorized Version means something with a spine in it: confortare, to make strong. Both occurrences are about speech. The woman of Tekoah tells David, “The word of my lord the king shall now be comfortable: for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and bad” (2Sa 14:17) — a king's ruling is comfortable because it is discerning and settles the matter. And the LORD answers the interceding angel “with good words and comfortable words” (Zec 1:13) after seventy years of silence over a ruined Jerusalem. In neither place is anyone made cosy. They are made strong. This is why the great comfort passages of Scripture are full of hard facts rather than soothing feelings: “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God” (Isa 40:1) opens a chapter about grass withering and the word of God standing for ever. And Paul roots all Christian consolation in God Himself, “who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble” (2Co 1:4). Comfort in Scripture is not the removal of the trouble; it is strength supplied inside it, and the strength comes by words.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines comfortable as being in a state of ease or moderate enjoyment; and also, giving comfort, administering comfort or consolation — a comfortable word being one that strengthens.

expand to see more

COM'FORTABLE, a. [See Comfort.]

1. Being in a state of ease, or moderate enjoyment; as a comfortable situation.

2. Admitting comfort; that may afford comfort.

3. Giving comfort; affording consolation; as comfortable words.

Let thy merciful kindness be for my comfort. The Latin confortare is to strengthen greatly, from fortis, strong.

Key Scripture

2 Samuel 14:17 — "Then thine handmaid said, The word of my lord the king shall now be comfortable: for as an angel of God, so is my lord the king to discern good and bad: therefore the LORD thy God will be with thee."

Zechariah 1:13 — "And the LORD answered the angel that talked with me with good words and comfortable words."

Isaiah 40:1 — "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God."

2 Corinthians 1:4 — "Who comforteth us in all our tribulation, that we may be able to comfort them which are in any trouble, by the comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God."

Modern Corruption

Comfort has migrated from strength-supplied to distress-avoided, and the church has followed the word down.

expand to see more

Once comfortable means unbothered, a comfortable church is one where nothing is said that would trouble anybody, and comfort ministry becomes the management of feeling. The Latin root judges the whole arrangement: confortare, to strengthen greatly. Zechariah's comfortable words were spoken over rubble and promised that the LORD would yet choose Jerusalem. They did not clear away one stone that morning. They put iron into men who had to keep building.

The therapeutic register makes this worse by reclassifying affliction as damage to be processed rather than a providence to be borne under God. Where Scripture says tribulation, the new vocabulary says trauma; where Scripture supplies strength, the new vocabulary supplies validation. 2 Corinthians 1:4 gives the true chain and it runs the other way: God comforts us in tribulation so that we may comfort others — the affliction is not wasted, and the comfort is transferable because it was never a mood. It was strength, and strength can be passed on.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin confortare, to strengthen greatly, from fortis, strong; Hebrew tob (H2896), good; Greek parakaleo (G3870), to call alongside.

expand to see more

Latin confortare, from con- and fortis — to strengthen greatly; the buried root, and the whole doctrine in one word.

Hebrew dabarim tobim dabarim nihumim — good words, comfortable words; Zechariah 1:13, spoken over ruins.

Greek parakaleo (G3870) — to call to one's side, to exhort, to comfort; the verb behind 2 Corinthians 1:4.

Greek paraklesis (G3874) — consolation, encouragement; the noun, and cousin to the Comforter of John 14:16.

Hebrew nacham (H5162) — to sigh, then to console; the word that opens Isaiah 40:1.

Usage

"“Good words and comfortable words” — spoken over rubble, and they built."

"“Comfort ye, comfort ye my people” — and then forty verses about grass withering."

"“The comfort wherewith we ourselves are comforted of God” — strength that can be handed on."
